1.5 — Movement II: Speed, deltaTime & Tuning

Your character moves — but it walks straight through walls, and it does not yet feel like anything. Today you take both problems seriously. You will compare every way Unity offers to move an object, learn why Time.deltaTime is what makes speed fair across machines, and tune your character until it feels right.

Read the Docs ~15 min

In Unity there is rarely just one way to solve a problem. Each of these four movement techniques exists because it solves a problem the others handle badly. Read the trade-offs — including which ones demand a component your character does not have yet:

TechniqueHow it worksNeeds a Rigidbody2D?Best for
transform.Translate(vector) Directly offsets the object's coordinates. Skips the physics engine entirely. No Simple top-down games, moving UI, linear projectiles, bullets without gravity
Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position) Sweeps the physics body to a target position, stopping cleanly against solid colliders. Yes Kinematic characters, moving platforms, top-down games that must never clip into walls
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity = vector Assigns a velocity vector to the physics body. The physics engine does the moving. Yes Snappy platformers, arcade physics, carrying momentum across surfaces
Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector) Applies a physical push or impulse, factoring in mass, drag, and inertia. Yes Jumping, thrusters, ice physics, knockback from explosions or enemy hits

Note what MovePosition buys you: it sweeps the body, meaning it checks the path rather than teleporting. That is the difference between walking into a wall and walking through one.

Socratic: Choosing the Right Tool for the Job

  1. You proved in 1.4 that transform.Translate walks through walls. In your own words, why does MovePosition not?
  2. Look at the third column. Three of these four options need a component your Player does not have yet. What would you have to add to your character, and where would you add it — on the Player, or on the child Sprite?
  3. Why would a game about a spaceship drifting through space prefer AddForce over Translate?
  4. The real question. This game is a top-down overworld where you explore, collect things, and later take damage from hazards. Which of these four does this game actually need? Argue for one, and name what you give up by choosing it.
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Examine how each function and language feature behaves in isolation, across completely different systems:

Example 1 — Fallback defaults versus Inspector overrides, on a racing kart:

// Code sets a fallback default, but whatever number is typed into the Inspector wins
[SerializeField] private float topSpeedMph = 45.0f;

Example 2 — Frame-rate independence, on a grandfather clock pendulum:

// Multiplying a rate by Time.deltaTime guarantees 30 degrees per SECOND,
// whether this runs on a 30 FPS phone or a 240 FPS gaming PC
float degreesThisFrame = swingSpeedDegreesPerSecond * Time.deltaTime;

Example 3 — Four movement signatures compared:

// 1. Direct coordinate offset (arcade / bullets / moving UI):
transform.Translate(new Vector3(stepDistance, 0, 0));

// 2. Kinematic sweep (stops cleanly against walls, never penetrates):
rb2d.MovePosition(rb2d.position + stepVector);

// 3. Velocity assignment (arcade platformers):
rb2d.linearVelocity = new Vector2(runSpeed, rb2d.linearVelocity.y);

// 4. Force impulse (thrusters / a jump launch):
rb2d.AddForce(Vector2.up * launchThrust, ForceMode2D.Impulse);

Predict Before Building

  1. A designer types 60.0 into the Inspector, but the C# file still says = 45.0f. Which number does the game use? What does that tell you about who is really in charge of a serialized field?
  2. Why does transform.Translate take a relative displacement ("how far to step right now"), while MovePosition takes an absolute target coordinate in world space?
  3. In signature 3, why does the code preserve rb2d.linearVelocity.y instead of simply setting both components? What would break if it zeroed them both?
Build Lab: Live-Tuning Workflow ~20 min

Numbers you guess at in the editor are almost never the numbers that feel right in motion. Professional designers tune while the game runs. Here is the workflow you will use for the rest of the year:

  1. Press Play in Unity, then walk around the overworld.
  2. While the game is still running, select the Player in the Hierarchy and change your speed knob in the Inspector. Walk again. Too sluggish?
  3. Try a much larger number. Notice how twitchy and uncontrollable it becomes.
  4. Bisect your way to a number that feels right for exploring a world this size. Try somewhere between 4 and 7 as a starting point.
  5. Write the number down, exit Play mode, and set that value in edit mode so it persists.
Remember the play-mode rule from 1.2: any value you change while the Play button is blue resets when you stop the game. Use play mode to find your number, then enter it in edit mode to keep it.

While you are tuning, also settle the design question you argued about in the Socratic section. If you decided to add a physics body, do it now — add the component in edit mode, then re-tune, because a physics-driven character will not feel the same as a translated one. Either choice is defensible. What matters is that you made it on purpose.

Bug Hunt: The deltaTime Abstraction

  1. Temporarily delete * Time.deltaTime from your movement calculation in Update(). Run the game and tap a direction key. Describe what happens in a single frame.
  2. A game runs at 60 FPS on your laptop and 240 FPS on a gaming desktop. Without Time.deltaTime, how much farther does the character travel per second on the faster machine?
  3. Why is Time.deltaTime best described as an abstraction? What messy detail is it hiding from you, and why is hiding it valuable?
  4. Set one speed knob far higher than the other — say 30 and 5 — and move diagonally. What does the character's path look like, and why?
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Asymmetric movement & feel

  1. Make your vertical speed a little slower than your horizontal speed. Walk around. In top-down 2D games, why do many classic RPGs do exactly this?
  2. Hold two direction keys to move diagonally. If both speeds are 5, the Pythagorean theorem says your diagonal speed is about 7.07 — you are moving 41% faster than intended. How could vector.normalized keep the speed constant in every direction, and what does "normalized" mean about the vector's length?
  3. If you chose a physics-based method, compare it against transform.Translate with the same speed value. Do they feel the same? If not, why not — what is the physics method doing that Translate is not?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare four ways to move an object in Unity: Translate, MovePosition, linearVelocity, AddForce
  • Say which of the four need a Rigidbody2D, and explain what a sweep does differently from a teleport
  • Justify the movement method you chose for this game, and name its cost
  • Explain how Time.deltaTime produces the same real-world speed at different frame rates
  • Explain the relationship between a code default and a serialized Inspector value
  • Save your tuned speeds and commit your changes
